Mister Utterson was sitting by his fireside one evening after dinner when he was surprised to receive a visit from Poole, Doctor Jekylls butler. <break time="0.8s" /> The butler, who was usually calm and proper, now looked so pale and nervous that Utterson asked him whether the doctor was ill. <break time="0.8s" /> I have been afraid for about a week, Poole said, and I can bear it no more, for I think there has been foul play. <break time="0.8s" /> Poole would not explain any further, but he begged the lawyer to come with him at once and see the matter for himself. <break time="0.8s" /> Utterson rose without another word, and the two men went out together into the wild, cold March night under a pale moon. <break time="0.8s" /> The wind made talking difficult, and it seemed to have swept the streets unusually bare of people that night. <break time="0.8s" /> Never had Utterson felt so sharp a wish to see and touch his fellow human beings, for a heavy fear was pressing on his mind. <break time="0.8s" /> When they reached the square, Poole stopped and wiped his brow with a red handkerchief, but it was fear, not the hurry, that had made him sweat. <break time="0.8s" /> Well, sir, here we are, he said, and God grant that there be nothing wrong.

The door was opened carefully on the chain, and inside the bright hall all the servants stood huddled together like a flock of frightened sheep. <break time="0.8s" /> At the sight of Utterson, the housemaid burst into tears, while the cook cried out, Bless God, it is Mister Utterson. <break time="0.8s" /> Poole took a candle and led the lawyer through the garden into the laboratory, where a flight of stairs led up to the cabinet door. <break time="0.8s" /> Come as quietly as you can, sir, whispered Poole, and if by any chance he asks you in, do not go. <break time="0.8s" /> Then he climbed the steps and knocked with an unsteady hand, calling out, Mister Utterson, sir, asking to see you. <break time="0.8s" /> A voice from inside answered in a complaining tone, Tell him I cannot see anyone, and Poole led the lawyer back to the kitchen. <break time="0.8s" /> Sir, said Poole, looking him in the eye, was that my masters voice, and Utterson, turning very pale, answered that it seemed much changed. <break time="0.8s" /> Changed, Have I been twenty years in this mans house to be fooled about his voice, cried Poole, his voice trembling with emotion. <break time="0.8s" /> No, sir, my master was done away with eight days ago, when we heard him cry out upon the name of God.
